reading.body:
DFW35 occupies 70,000 square feet of technical space in Richardson, Texas, but the operator has not published a megawatt figure, making it impossible to assess whether the facility can support AI workloads that require sustained high-density electrical loads.

Floor space alone does not establish compute capacity. A 70,000-square-foot building might hold a few dozen racks at low power density or hundreds at high density. Without a power specification, DFW35 cannot be ranked among the 13 Texas facilities that have disclosed megawatt capacity, and it falls outside the 389 MW total compiled for the state. The three certifications on record, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, and ISO 9001, establish security and compliance standards but say nothing about power infrastructure, redundancy tier, or whether the building is configured for accelerator-intensive workloads.

Texas has 133 mapped facilities in this index, yet only 13 have published power figures. DFW35 is among the 120 that have not. For someone evaluating AI training or large-scale inference capacity in the Dallas-Fort Worth region, the absence of a power specification is the limiting fact. The facility's tenants and workload types are not disclosed, so neither its current use nor its suitability for future AI deployment can be determined from available data.
